nameStory: The name 'candytuft' comes from the plant's original home in Candia (now Crete), where early botanists first described these sweet-looking flowers. The 'tuft' part refers to the dense, rounded clusters of tiny white blooms that look like little puffs of cotton candy. 'Perennial' distinguishes this long-lived garden favorite from its annual cousin, while 'evergreen' (what sempervirens means in Latin) hints at its year-round green foliage.
description: Perennial candytuft is a low-growing, spreading shrub that forms dense mats of dark green foliage topped with brilliant white flower clusters. This Mediterranean native typically grows 6-12 inches tall but can spread 12-18 inches wide, creating neat cushions of color in spring gardens. The plant stays green all year long, making it popular with gardeners who want something attractive even in winter. You'll mainly find this as an escaped garden plant in New England, since it's not native to our region but sometimes spreads from landscaping.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Dense, flat-topped clusters of tiny white flowers, each with four petals arranged in a cross shape typical of the mustard family. The flower heads are about 1-2 inches across and feel papery to the touch, with a sweet, honey-like fragrance.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Small, narrow, dark green leaves that feel thick and leathery, staying green through winter. They're arranged alternately along the stem and have smooth edges with no teeth or lobes.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms low, spreading mats or cushions that hug the ground, with woody stems at the base. The plant spreads outward more than upward, creating dense carpets of foliage.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Small, flat, heart-shaped seed pods typical of mustard family plants. They start green and turn brown when ripe, splitting open to release tiny seeds.

habitat: In New England, you'll occasionally find perennial candytuft escaped from gardens into nearby disturbed areas, roadsides, or waste places. It prefers well-drained, sunny spots and can tolerate poor, rocky soils. Since it's not native here, it's most likely to pop up near residential areas where it was originally planted as an ornamental.

seasonality.spring: Peak blooming time with masses of white flower clusters covering the plant from April through May. This is when the plant is most noticeable and easiest to identify from a distance.
seasonality.summer: Flowers fade but the evergreen foliage remains prominent. Seed pods develop and ripen, turning from green to brown as summer progresses.
seasonality.fall: Still green and leafy while most other plants are dying back. Seeds may be dispersing from the dried pods, potentially creating new plants nearby.
seasonality.winter: Remains green and recognizable under snow, making it one of the few non-native plants you can still identify in the dormant season. The woody stems and persistent leaves are visible even in harsh weather.

funFact: Despite being called 'candytuft,' this plant is actually a member of the mustard family, making it more closely related to broccoli and radishes than to any kind of candy - though early gardeners thought the sweet-scented flower clusters looked good enough to eat!
confusionNotes: The dense white flower clusters might be confused with sweet alyssum, but candytuft has larger individual flowers arranged in flatter heads, and its leaves stay thick and green all winter while sweet alyssum dies back. Remember: candytuft keeps its 'candy' (green leaves) all year round.
contextualKnowledge: Though beautiful and popular in gardens, perennial candytuft isn't native to New England - it's originally from southern Europe around the Mediterranean. Most plants you encounter will be garden escapes rather than truly wild populations, so finding one might mean you're near a current or former residential area.
compareHints: Perennial candytuft differs from its relative wild candytuft by being evergreen (wild candytuft is annual and dies completely each year) and having consistently white flowers in denser, more rounded clusters. While wild candytuft can have pinkish or purplish flowers and grows more upright, perennial candytuft always stays white and spreads in low mats.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Wild candytuft differs from its garden cousin (Iberis sempervirens) by being an annual that dies each year rather than a perennial, having more irregular flower clusters, and showing more variation in petal sizes within each flower head.
